idiom_name: class implementing the interface + hand-written forwarders (`implements` checks, never generates)
implementation_notes: TypeScript's `implements` clause is only a check that the class can be treated as the interface type - the handbook warns explicitly that it does not change the class or its methods - so a wrapper must still write every forwarder, and one that merely declares `implements Store` fails to compile until its members exist. Where no wrapper class is needed, structural typing acts as the type-level equivalent: any object of the right shape satisfies the interface, so an object literal or a spread (`{ ...delegate, extra() {} }`) can act as the delegating object; the `mixins` chapter covers copying implementations between prototypes when several small behaviour sets must be combined. At run time the only transparent, generating mechanism is `Proxy`, which is interception rather than plain delegation.
pitfalls: `implements` is erased at compile time: it produces no forwarding code and does not change the class's inferred type, so believing otherwise means the wrapper silently lacks members until the compiler objects.

Spread/`Object.assign` delegation copies own enumerable properties once: prototype methods, accessors and later changes to the delegate are not picked up, and the copy loses the delegate's identity and prototype.

`private`/`#` members and interfaces carrying private brands cannot be re-implemented by a wrapper at all, and structural typing lets an unrelated object satisfy the interface - the wrapper's declared type is no proof that the delegate is the intended implementation.
